title: Ashton Park and the Remaking of South Palm Bay — What It Actually Means If You Own or Want Land Here
metaTitle: Ashton Park Palm Bay: What It Means for Land Buyers
metaDescription: A $2.5B development is coming to Micco Road in South Palm Bay. Here's the honest picture of what Ashton Park means for nearby land values, utilities, and lot buyers.
subtitle: A $2.5 billion, 1,400-acre project is taking shape on Micco Road — here's the honest, local read on what it means for people who own land nearby or are thinking about buying a lot in South Palm Bay.
content:
South Palm Bay is being remade around the St. Johns Heritage Parkway and Micco Road corridor — and land owners are the quiet story inside it.

Every few years a project comes along that changes the map of a city. In South Palm Bay, that project is Ashton Park — a roughly 1,400-acre, $2.5 billion mixed-use development planned by DIX Developments along Micco Road, near the St. Johns Heritage Parkway. The developer's plans describe something close to a new town: on the order of 3,700 single-family homes, around 800 apartments, and up to 6 million square feet of commercial and flex space, anchored by a 49-acre downtown district and a site set aside for a future school. Local outlet The Palm Bayer profiled the project in its piece Redefining Palm Bay: The Astonishing Vision of Ashton Park.

That is a genuinely big deal for a part of Palm Bay that, until recently, was mostly quiet residential streets and vacant lots. But if you own land nearby — or you're weighing whether to buy a lot out here — the honest question isn't "is this exciting?" It's "what does it actually mean for me?" Here's the straight version, from people who have worked this market for 20+ years.

What Ashton Park Actually Is (and Isn't Yet)

Ashton Park is real and moving. Public records show the developer has already closed on the land in large pieces — a 1,134-acre acquisition reported at about $74 million and an earlier 302-acre purchase around $15.6 million. Approvals are in place and it's heading toward groundbreaking. It's not a rumor or a rendering that never gets built.

What it isn't, yet, is finished. A project this size is a phased buildout measured in a decade or more, not a season. The downtown district, the commercial square footage, the thousands of rooftops — those arrive in stages through the late 2020s and into the 2030s. If you're picturing a bustling town center next spring, adjust the timeline. The value story for land owners is a patient one, not an overnight one.

Ashton Park also isn't alone. Just to its west, SunTerra Lakes — roughly 1,900 acres with about 3,246 planned homes and a 125-acre lake — is heading toward construction on the same broad corridor. Two master-planned communities of that scale, side by side, is what makes South Palm Bay one of the most-watched growth stories on the Space Coast right now.

What It Means If You Already Own Land Nearby

If you bought a lot in South or Southeast Palm Bay years ago and it's just been sitting, this is the news you want to understand. Here's the honest mechanics of how a project like this affects nearby raw land:

  • Infrastructure follows rooftops. Thousands of new homes require water, sewer, and roads. As the city and county extend utilities and widen roads to serve Ashton Park and SunTerra Lakes, some previously well-and-septic areas move closer to city water and sewer — and in our own pricing, city water adds roughly $20,000 and city water + sewer roughly $40,000 to a lot's value. A utility extension near your parcel is one of the few events that can reprice it before the broader market notices.
  • Comps rise with activity. When national builders are paying real money for lots on a corridor, nearby raw-land comparables tend to drift up with them. That doesn't guarantee your specific lot appreciates — location, unit, zoning, and buildability all matter — but the direction of pressure is upward, not down.
  • Not every nearby lot benefits equally. This is the part most hype leaves out. A lot that's genuinely close to the new corridor with a path to utilities is in a different position than a landlocked parcel with no services. And to be blunt: the Port Malabar "Compound" (Units 51, 52, and 53) is not buildable and has no utilities — proximity to a big project doesn't change that. If you want to know honestly where your specific lot sits, that's a five-minute phone call, not a guess.

What It Means If You're Thinking About Buying a Lot

For buyers, land is the affordable way in — not because a lot is a house, but because it's the entry point. A brand-new home in this part of Palm Bay generally starts north of $300,000. Our vacant residential lots start around $41,000 in Southwest Palm Bay and about $45,000 in the Southeast — the value quadrants nearest this growth, with Ashton Park itself on the Southeast side. You'll still build when you're ready, but locking in the land now, at today's price, is how people get a foothold in a fast-growing area long before a $300,000 mortgage is on the table.

And you don't need a bank to do it. We sell lots with owner financing: as little as 30% down for an option contract or 40% down to take the deed at closing, at 10% APR over up to 10 years, with personal approval — we look at the person, not just a credit score. The deed transfers to you once 40% of the price is paid, there's no prepayment penalty, and no balloon.

There's also a protection most buyers don't get anywhere else: our lot exchange guarantee. If a lot you buy turns out to have an issue, you can exchange it for another lot of the same price category and size at no extra cost beyond the deed-transfer fee — even if values have risen since. In a fast-moving market, that safety net matters.

The Honest Bottom Line

Ashton Park is a real, funded, city-shaping project, and it's part of a broader wave — SunTerra Lakes, the St. Johns Heritage Parkway build-out, the Malabar Road widening — that is steadily raising the profile of South and Southwest Palm Bay. Add Florida's no state income tax and Palm Bay's ranking as the #13 most affordable city in America (the only Florida city in the national top 20), and the long-term case for owning land here is genuinely strong.

What we won't do is promise you that any single lot will double in value because a development is nearby. It doesn't work that cleanly, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling. What we will do is tell you exactly where a specific lot sits relative to this growth — utilities, buildability, quadrant, and price — so you can make a clear-eyed decision.

faqs.q: Where is Ashton Park being built in Palm Bay?
faqs.a: Ashton Park is a roughly 1,400-acre, ~$2.5 billion mixed-use development by DIX Developments along Micco Road in South/Southeast Palm Bay, near the St. Johns Heritage Parkway. Plans call for around 3,700 single-family homes, ~800 apartments, up to 6 million square feet of commercial/flex space, and a 49-acre downtown district, built out in phases over the coming years.

faqs.q: Will Ashton Park make my nearby Palm Bay lot worth more?
faqs.a: It can, but it's not automatic. Large developments pull utilities, roads, and builder activity toward a corridor, which tends to push nearby raw-land comps upward and can add real value when city water or sewer reaches a previously well-and-septic lot. But location, unit, zoning, and buildability all matter, and some parcels benefit far more than others. Call 321-333-7230 for an honest read on your specific lot.

A lot isn't a finished home — you'll still build when you're ready — but buying land near the growth corridor is the affordable way to get a foothold before prices climb.
